title: The Split-Attention Effect
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: This is the third edition of Jamie Lee Clark's DistillED series on Cognitive Load Theory. He defines split attention as the cost students pay when they must combine two or more sources of information separated in space or time, holding one in working memory while they search for the match in the other. The effect was discovered by accident when Tarmizi and Sweller found geometry worked examples failed until the solution steps were written onto the diagram. Clark lists what the effect is and is not, citing meta-analyses by Ginns and by Schroeder and Cenkci and the expertise-reversal finding that integration can hurt knowledgeable learners. He gives five steps: spot look-away moments, put words where the eyes are, say it while they see it, link what you cannot move, and teach students to join it up. The practical ask is to fix one slide or worksheet tomorrow.
points: Clark frames split attention as extraneous load caused by layout and search, not by distraction or by the difficulty of the content itself.
The effect surfaced when geometry worked examples only helped once solution steps were written onto the diagram beside the angles they described.
Meta-analyses find a clear benefit from integrating sources, but it shrinks or reverses for learners who already know the material, so it matters most for novices and complex content.

Five steps move from spotting look-away moments to placing labels beside what they describe, aligning explanation with the visual in time, linking fixed materials, and teaching students to number and connect chunks.
The takeaway is a small, immediate task: find one place in tomorrow's slides or worksheet where students look back and forth, and move the words next to the thing they describe.
quotes: Split attention happens when students have to combine two or more sources of information that have been separated, either in space or in time.
That searching and holding adds extraneous load, which is load caused by how the material is presented rather than by the content itself
The problem was the layout. As in most textbooks, the solution steps sat underneath the diagram, so students kept looking back and forth to find which angle each line referred to.
In one study, placing definitions of key words directly within a passage helped Year 5 students and less confident English learners understand what they were reading.

The message for classrooms is clear: Split attention is most likely to hinder learning when students have limited prior knowledge, the material is complex, and understanding requires them to mentally connect separate sources of information.
Most split attention is built in before the lesson starts, in the slide, the worksheet or the method sheet.
The goal isn’t to make complex content simple. It’s to remove unnecessary searching so students can focus their effort on understanding the content itself.
Show students how to join split material up themselves: number each chunk of text, put the same number on the part of the diagram it describes, and draw a line between them.
